name: Nam
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct, fragmentarily attested from one manuscript (Thomas 1951); no phonology of stress exists

sources.citation: Thomas, F. W. 1948. Nam, an ancient language of the Sino-Tibetan borderland. (Publications of the Philological Society 14.) London: Oxford University Press. [archive.org Digital Library of India scan in.ernet.dli.2015.529352]
sources.note: Nothing. The phonological discussion (script/orthography, prefixes, initials, finals, vowel alternation, pp. ~109-124) contains no statement on word stress or accent. Only prosodic remark, p. 123: the i/ihi, u/uhu, e/ehe, o/oho vowel doubling 'might be regarded as corresponding to one or other of the "tones" of Chinese or Indo-Chinese languages; but it certainly is not employed as a means of discriminating homonyms.' Full-text grep for accent/stress/prosod yields no hits about the language's prosody.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Nam language' (reference list: Thomas JRAS 1928, 1939; Thomas 1948; Lalou 1939 Journal Asiatique 231; Shafer 1963 Monumenta Serica 22:169-184; Wen You 1981 Minzu Yuwen 1:16-25; Chen Zongxiang 1994, 1997 Sichuan Zangxue yanjiu; Ikeda Takumi 2012 in Medieval Tibeto-Burman Languages IV, 111-119)
sources.note: Nothing; confirms the language is known only from Tibetan-script transcriptions in Dunhuang fragments (British Library, BnF); all secondary literature concerns decipherment/identification.

sources.citation: Ikeda, Takumi. 2012. Highlights in the decipherment of the Nam language. In Nathan W. Hill (ed.), Medieval Tibeto-Burman Languages IV, 111-119. Leiden: Brill.
